Much has already been written and said about President Trump's decision on Friday to ease sanctions on Russian diesel in an effort to bring down fuel costs ahead of the US midterm elections. I have made a point of keeping this feed focused on markets rather than politics, and intend to continue doing so.

However, the economic pressure behind the decision is clear, with diesel prices hovering near USD 200 per barrel and US consumers facing exceptionally high fuel costs. Russian supplies on the scale being discussed are unlikely to have more than a limited impact, especially compared to the potential political fallout from this decision. Indeed, New York ULSD futures fell just 3% on Friday to USD 4.74 per gallon, remaining within their recent 50-cent trading range. More importantly, additional Russian supplies would do little to address the underlying problem. The global distillate market remains exceptionally tight, primarily because of disrupted refinery operations and product exports from the Persian Gulf, compounded by reduced Russian refinery output.

The distinction matters: crude oil shipments from the Gulf have recovered significantly, but refined product flows remain severely constrained. With substantial refining capacity still offline, restoring crude supply alone will not resolve the diesel shortage. Moreover, redirecting Russian exports towards the US would do little to increase overall global availability. A sustained easing of distillate prices will ultimately require the restoration of refining capacity and product exports, particularly from the Middle East.

COT on #commodities: A broad rebound following two weeks of losses did little to change the selling bias among managed money accounts. According to the latest COT report, covering the week to 6 October, when the Bloomberg Commodity Index rose 1.2%, these traders remained net sellers across several key markets, including crude oil, natural gas, gold, copper, corn and cotton. Buying was concentrated in fewer contracts, led by sugar and soybeans. 

Energy: The combined WTI and Brent crude oil net long was cut for a third consecutive week, falling by 23k contracts to a two-month low of 313k, while the natural gas net short jumped to a two-and-a-half-year high.

Metals: The COMEX gold net long fell to a three-month low of 115k contracts, highlighting the contrast between short-term momentum traders and longer-term investors, whose continued ETF accumulation has lifted holdings to a four-year high. In copper, long liquidation accelerated despite a modest weekly price gain, with funds cutting their net long by 22% to a three-month low of 64.5k contracts.

Agriculture: Corn longs continued to be reduced following last month's record high, with a 60k-contract cut to a still elevated 317.4k occurring ahead of Friday's bearish WASDE surprise, which triggered the biggest one-day slump since 2023. Elsewhere, a 10.5% surge in sugar futures drove a 13% increase in the net long to 257.4k contracts, just below its 2023 record.
